hints: Notice that urea is the only product, so no atoms can be lost or gained. Think about what that tells you about the starting material.
Count the atoms in one molecule of urea, $\text{CO(NH}_2\text{)}_2$, and remember ammonium is $\text{NH}_4^+$. What atoms must be left for cyanate?
Use charge balance next. With a $+1$ ammonium ion present, what charge must the cyanate ion carry to make a neutral salt?
walkthrough:
**Use atom conservation**

This is an isomerisation with only one product, so the reactant and product must contain exactly the same atoms. Start by counting atoms in urea.

$$\text{CO(NH}_2\text{)}_2 = \text{C}_1\text{O}_1\text{N}_2\text{H}_4$$

**Subtract the ammonium ion**

Ammonium cyanate is $\text{NH}_4^+$ plus cyanate. Remove $\text{N}_1\text{H}_4$ from the total to leave what cyanate must supply.

$$\text{C}_1\text{O}_1\text{N}_2\text{H}_4 - \text{N}_1\text{H}_4 = \text{C}_1\text{O}_1\text{N}_1$$

**Balance the charge**

The salt must be neutral overall. Ammonium is $+1$, so cyanate must be $-1$ to cancel it. That gives $\text{OCN}^-$ which contains C, O and one N.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{CON}_2^-$ suggests two N atoms in the anion. Combined with $\text{NH}_4^+$ this would give three N atoms in total, but urea only has two N atoms. It also misplaces the atoms.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{CON}_2^{2-}$ has both the wrong number of N atoms and the wrong charge. A 2- anion would need two ammonium ions to balance, which would give far too many H and N atoms compared to urea.
options.C: Correct. $\text{OCN}^-$ contains $\text{C}_1\text{O}_1\text{N}_1$ with a 1- charge. Added to $\text{NH}_4^+$, the total is $\text{C}_1\text{O}_1\text{N}_2\text{H}_4$, exactly the composition of urea, and the charges balance to neutral.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{OCN}^{2-}$ has the right atoms but the wrong charge. A 2- charge cannot be balanced by a single $\text{NH}_4^+$ ion, and students choosing this often forget to check charge neutrality.
